subject: business-studies
title: Capacity and Capacity Utilisation
welcome_lead: Find the sweet spot between idle capacity and overstretched plant.
meta_desc: A-Level Operations: capacity utilisation, full capacity, under-utilisation.
final_note: High utilisation cuts unit cost; too high risks quality and breakdowns.

concepts.def: Maximum output a firm can produce in a given period.
Current output divided by maximum capacity, as a percentage.
Operating below full capacity - unit costs rise.
Pushing beyond comfortable capacity - quality slips.
Costs that do not vary with output in the short run.
Total cost divided by units produced.

walkthroughs.body_html: Utilisation = (current output / maximum capacity) x 100. A factory producing 8,000 of 10,000 capacity runs at 80 percent.
Fixed costs are spread over more units as utilisation rises, so unit cost falls. But quality, maintenance and staff stress all suffer above roughly 90 percent.
Firms can boost demand (marketing, price cuts), rationalise (close sites), subcontract spare capacity to other firms, or develop new products to fill the lines.

mcqs.q: What is operations management concerned with?
options: Operations management is the same as general management.

The design and control of the production process and business operations — converting inputs into outputs efficiently. It includes capacity, quality, supply chain, and process improvement.

mcqs.q: What is Taylor's theory of scientific management?
options: Operations management is only about manufacturing factories.
Taylor said workers are motivated by recognition and teamwork.
Taylor invented the assembly line at Ford.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between fixed and variable costs?
options: Fixed costs do not change with output level (e.g. rent, salaries); variable costs change in proportion to output (e.g. raw materials, hourly wages).
